questions.stem: The role of financial management is best described as:
options: planning and monitoring a business's finances to meet its goals
recording each sale and purchase so the tax return can be lodged on time
setting the prices of products so that they match those of competitors
deciding which employees will be hired, trained and promoted each year
questions.explanation: Financial management plans, sources, monitors and controls the business's funds so that it can achieve its goals. Recording transactions is bookkeeping, only one small input into financial management.

questions.stem: Why is financial management described as interdependent with the other key business functions?
options: it is the only function that is required by law to keep written records
every function needs funds, and finance depends on their results
the finance manager directly supervises the staff in every other department
finance decisions are made only after the other functions have spent their budgets
questions.explanation: Marketing, operations and human resources all need funds to carry out their plans, and their results generate the revenue and costs that finance must manage. The finance manager does not usually supervise other departments' staff.

questions.stem: The financial objective of liquidity refers to a business's ability to:
options: keep its costs low relative to the revenue that it earns
meet its short-term financial commitments as they fall due
meet its long-term debts and remain in business over time
earn the greatest possible profit from its available resources
questions.explanation: Liquidity is about short-term commitments, usually those due within 12 months, such as paying suppliers and wages. Meeting long-term debts is solvency.

questions.stem: The financial objective of solvency refers to a business's ability to:
options: convert its inventory into cash quickly
lower its expenses as a share of sales
meet its long-term financial commitments
pay its suppliers within the agreed terms
questions.explanation: Solvency concerns the long term: whether the business can meet its debts over time, which depends heavily on how much it relies on borrowed funds. Paying suppliers on time is a liquidity matter.

questions.stem: The financial objective of efficiency is best described as:
options: achieving the business's results with the lowest costs
earning more revenue than the business's competitors in the same industry
holding enough cash in the bank to pay every bill as soon as it arrives
funding all of the business's assets from the owners' own contributions
questions.explanation: Efficiency is the ability to minimise costs and manage assets so that the business achieves its results with the fewest resources. Holding enough cash to pay bills is liquidity.

questions.stem: A Newcastle engineering firm keeps $2 million in a low-interest bank account so that it can always pay its bills. Which conflict between financial objectives does this show?
options: high liquidity may reduce profitability, as the idle cash earns little
high solvency may reduce liquidity, as the cash cannot be spent quickly
high efficiency may reduce solvency, as costs are cut too far
high profitability may reduce efficiency, as more staff are needed
questions.explanation: Cash held for safety improves liquidity, but it earns a low return compared with investing it in productive assets, so profitability may suffer. Cash is the most liquid asset, so holding it cannot reduce liquidity.

questions.stem: A Penrith retailer borrows heavily to open five new stores, expecting the extra sales to lift profit. Which statement best evaluates this decision against its financial objectives?
options: solvency improves, because the new stores are assets that can be sold later
liquidity improves, because a loan is repaid in full when the stores open
efficiency must rise, because more stores always lower the cost of each sale
profitability may rise, but the higher debt weakens solvency and adds risk
questions.explanation: Debt can fund growth that raises profit, but more borrowing raises interest costs and reliance on lenders, which weakens solvency if sales fall short. Loan repayments are an ongoing commitment, so they do not improve liquidity.

questions.stem: Which action would most directly improve a business's liquidity?
options: collecting money owed by customers more quickly
taking out a 20-year loan to buy a new factory
increasing the dividend paid to shareholders
buying extra inventory in bulk to cut its price
questions.explanation: Collecting receivables faster brings cash in sooner, so the business can meet its short-term commitments. Buying extra inventory ties cash up in stock, and higher dividends pay cash out.

questions.stem: Investment appraisal is best described as:
options: judging whether an investment's expected returns justify its cost
estimating the market value of the business's shares on the stock exchange
checking that the business's tax return correctly records its investments
measuring how many units a new machine can produce in a single shift
questions.explanation: Investment appraisal compares the expected returns of a project, such as new equipment, with its costs and risks before funds are committed. Valuing the business's shares is a different task.

questions.stem: Why should a business carry out investment appraisal before sourcing finance for a project?
options: because lenders are legally barred from lending to businesses without one
because it fixes the interest rate that the bank will charge on the loan
to make sure the project can be paid for entirely from retained profit
to avoid taking on debt or issuing shares for a project that will not pay off
questions.explanation: Appraisal shows whether the project's returns are likely to cover its cost, including the cost of the finance itself, before the business commits to repayments or gives up ownership. It does not set the bank's interest rate.

questions.stem: A Dubbo bakery is considering a new oven costing $120,000. It expects the oven to add $30,000 a year to net cash inflows. What is the payback period?
options: 5 years
6 years
4 years
3 years
questions.explanation: Payback period = cost / annual net cash inflow = $120,000 / $30,000 = 4 years. A shorter payback period means the investment recovers its cost sooner and carries less risk.

questions.stem: A project costs $200,000 and is expected to earn $30,000 profit a year. The business can borrow the full amount at 8% a year. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: the 6.7% annual return is below the 8% cost of borrowing, so the project should be rejected
the 15% annual return is below the 8% cost of borrowing once tax is taken into account
the project's return cannot be judged until the loan has been fully repaid
the 15% annual return exceeds the 8% cost of borrowing, so the project may be worthwhile
questions.explanation: Annual return = $30,000 / $200,000 = 0.15, or 15%. Because this is above the 8% interest cost, the project is likely to add to profit, although risks must still be weighed. The 6.7% figure comes from dividing the wrong way.

questions.stem: Which is an internal source of finance?
options: retained profit
a bank overdraft
a share issue
a lease
questions.explanation: Internal finance comes from within the business, such as profits kept rather than paid out and the sale of assets. Overdrafts, leases and share issues all come from outsiders.

questions.stem: Which is a key advantage of using retained profit rather than external finance?
options: it is always available in whatever amount the business needs
it raises the business's profit by the amount reinvested
it allows the business to pay larger dividends to its owners
there is no interest to pay and no ownership is given up
questions.explanation: Retained profit costs no interest and does not dilute ownership. Its limit is that the amount available depends on past profits, and reinvesting it means owners receive less in dividends.

questions.stem: A Wollongong printing company sells an unused warehouse for $800,000 and uses the cash to buy new digital presses. This source of finance is:
options: external, through equity finance
external, through a sale and leaseback
internal, through retained profit
internal, through the sale of assets
questions.explanation: Selling an asset the business owns raises funds from within the business. It is not a sale and leaseback, because the company does not go on renting the warehouse after selling it.

questions.stem: Debt finance is best described as:
options: profits that have been kept in the business rather than paid out
money a business receives from selling assets it no longer needs
borrowed funds that must be repaid, usually with interest
funds provided by the owners in return for a share of the business
questions.explanation: Debt is borrowed money that must be repaid, with interest, by agreed dates. Funds provided in exchange for ownership are equity.

questions.stem: A bank overdraft allows a business to:
options: borrow a fixed sum that is repaid in instalments over several years
use an asset owned by another business in return for regular payments
sell the money owed by its customers to another firm for immediate cash
withdraw more than the balance of its account, up to an agreed limit
questions.explanation: An overdraft lets the account go below zero up to a limit, giving flexible short-term funds, with interest charged only on the amount overdrawn. A fixed sum repaid over years is a term loan.

questions.stem: A Coffs Harbour landscaping business often runs short of cash for a few weeks before large customer payments arrive. Which source of finance best suits this need?
options: a bank overdraft
a 25-year mortgage
a public share issue
a five-year lease
questions.explanation: An overdraft is designed for short, irregular cash shortfalls and is repaid as cash comes in. A mortgage or share issue suits long-term needs, such as buying property or funding expansion.

questions.stem: Factoring involves a business:
options: paying a monthly fee to use equipment owned by a finance company
issuing new shares to a small group of private investors
selling its accounts receivable to a factor for immediate cash
borrowing against the value of a building that it owns outright
questions.explanation: A factoring company buys the business's accounts receivable at a discount and then collects the debts itself. Borrowing against a building is a mortgage.

questions.stem: A Tamworth wholesaler factors $50,000 of accounts receivable. The factoring company charges 4% of their value. How much cash does the wholesaler receive?
questions.explanation: The factor keeps 4% of $50,000, which is $2,000, so the wholesaler receives $50,000 - $2,000 = $48,000. The business gets cash now, but at the cost of the discount.

questions.stem: Which is a disadvantage of factoring compared with waiting for customers to pay?
options: the business must make repayments with interest over several years
the business must give the factoring company a share of ownership
the business must pay the factor a fixed monthly fee for five years
the business receives less than the full value of the money owed
questions.explanation: The factor's discount means the business gives up part of what it is owed in return for immediate cash. Factoring is a sale of receivables, not a loan repaid with interest or a long-term fee arrangement.

questions.stem: A mortgage is:
options: a credit limit on a business credit card
a share issue made to existing owners
a long-term loan secured against property
a short-term loan with no security at all
questions.explanation: A mortgage is a long-term loan, often 20 years or more, secured by property; if repayments are not made, the lender can sell the property. Because it is secured, its interest rate is usually lower than unsecured borrowing.

questions.stem: A Bathurst manufacturer leases its delivery trucks instead of buying them. Which is the main advantage of leasing?
options: it pays less in total than it would by buying the trucks outright
it has no further payments to make once the trucks are delivered
it can use the trucks without paying their full cost up front
it gains ownership of the trucks as soon as the lease is signed
questions.explanation: Leasing lets the business use an asset in return for regular payments, keeping cash free for other purposes. Over the full term, lease payments often total more than the purchase price, and the business does not own the asset.

questions.stem: Why do business credit cards usually suit only small, short-term purchases?
options: they require the business to give the bank a share of its profits
their interest rates are high if the balance is not repaid quickly
they can be used only to pay wages and superannuation to employees
they must be secured against the business owner's home or property
questions.explanation: Credit cards are convenient and often have an interest-free period, but unpaid balances attract high interest rates, making them costly for large or long-term needs. They are generally unsecured.

questions.stem: A business needs $2 million to build a factory it will use for 30 years. Which matching of finance to need is most appropriate, and why?
options: a mortgage, because a long-term asset should be funded by long-term finance
an overdraft, because it is flexible and interest is paid only on what is used
factoring, because selling receivables raises the funds without any discount
a credit card, because it gives an interest-free period on large purchases
questions.explanation: Long-term assets should be funded by long-term finance so that repayments are spread over the asset's useful life. Funding a factory with an overdraft would expose the business to repayment on demand and high short-term rates.

questions.stem: Equity finance is best described as:
options: funds raised by selling the business's accounts receivable
funds provided by suppliers who allow delayed payment
funds provided by owners in exchange for a share of ownership
funds borrowed from a bank that are repaid with interest
questions.explanation: Equity comes from owners, such as through private investment or a public share issue, and gives them part ownership and a claim on profits. It does not have to be repaid like a loan.

questions.stem: A private equity firm invests $5 million in an unlisted Sydney software company in return for a 40% stake. Which is the main disadvantage for the founders?
options: they must repay the $5 million with interest within five years
they must list the company's shares on the stock exchange at once
they lose the protection of limited liability for the company's debts
they give up part of the ownership, control and future profits
questions.explanation: Private equity investors take an ownership stake and often a say in decisions, so the founders' share of control and future profits falls. Unlike a loan, the money is not repaid with interest.

questions.stem: Which is an advantage of raising finance through a public share issue?
options: it is cheaper and faster to arrange than a small business overdraft
the company no longer has to publish its annual financial reports
large sums can be raised with no interest or repayment
the existing owners keep complete control over all business decisions
questions.explanation: Selling shares to the public can raise large amounts with no repayment or interest. However, it is costly and slow, dilutes existing owners' control and brings strict reporting and disclosure obligations.

questions.stem: A listed company wants to raise $50 million for expansion. Its debt is already high relative to equity. Which source is most suitable, and why?
options: a share issue, because it adds funds without raising the company's debt
a bank loan, because interest is cheaper than paying any dividends
a credit card, because it gives the most flexible short-term funds
factoring, because it turns all future sales into cash immediately
questions.explanation: Already-high debt means more borrowing would weaken solvency and raise risk, so equity is the safer choice despite diluting ownership. Factoring only converts existing receivables, not future sales, and could not raise $50 million for expansion.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares debt and equity finance?
options: debt is available only to companies; equity is available only to sole traders
debt must be repaid with interest; equity gives investors ownership instead
debt gives lenders ownership; equity must be repaid with interest by a set date
debt is always cheaper; equity is always riskier for the business that raises it
questions.explanation: Lenders receive interest and repayment but no ownership, while equity investors receive part ownership and a share of profits but no guaranteed repayment. Sole traders cannot issue shares, so equity through shares is a company option.

questions.stem: A company with aggregated turnover under $50 million is a base rate entity and pays company tax at 25%. Its net profit before tax is $400,000. How much company tax does it pay?
questions.explanation: Company tax = 25% x $400,000 = $100,000. The $120,000 figure applies the full 30% rate, and $300,000 is the profit left after tax.

questions.stem: How can the company tax rate influence a business's financial management?
options: a higher rate removes the need to prepare financial statements
a lower rate leaves more after-tax profit to retain or pay as dividends
a lower rate raises the interest rate charged on the business's loans
a higher rate increases the business's revenue from sales
questions.explanation: Company tax is paid from profit, so a lower rate leaves more profit to reinvest as retained profit or distribute to shareholders. Tax rates do not set the interest rates that lenders charge.

questions.stem: A business has a $500,000 variable-rate loan. The interest rate rises from 6% to 8% a year. What is the effect on its annual interest expense?
options: it falls by $10,000, from $40,000 to $30,000
it rises by $10,000, from $30,000 to $40,000
it rises by $20,000, from $30,000 to $50,000
it rises by $2,000, from $30,000 to $32,000
questions.explanation: Interest at 6% = $30,000 and at 8% = $40,000, so the expense rises by $10,000, reducing profit. Higher interest rates make debt more costly and may make equity or retained profit relatively more attractive.

questions.stem: An Albury firm must pay 65,000 US dollars (USD) for imported equipment. Before it pays, the Australian dollar falls from 0.70 USD to 0.65 USD. What happens to the cost in Australian dollars?
options: it stays the same, at $65,000 throughout
it rises, from about $92,857 to $100,000
it falls, from about $100,000 to $92,857
it rises, from about $42,250 to $45,500
questions.explanation: Cost in Australian dollars = 65,000 / exchange rate: 65,000 / 0.70 is about $92,857, and 65,000 / 0.65 = $100,000. A depreciating dollar makes imports dearer; multiplying instead of dividing gives the $42,250 figure.

questions.stem: During a contraction in the business cycle, a business is most likely to:
options: find that its interest rates are fixed by law for the rest of the year
find lenders more cautious, so it delays expansion and builds cash reserves
find lenders keen to lend, so it borrows heavily to build new factories
find its sales rising, so it reduces its overdraft and pays higher dividends
questions.explanation: Falling sales and greater uncertainty in a contraction lead lenders to tighten credit and businesses to protect liquidity. Heavy borrowing for expansion is more typical of a boom.

questions.stem: Under the Corporations Act 2001, which companies generally must prepare audited annual financial reports and lodge them with ASIC?
options: all sole traders and partnerships that employ staff
only companies that are making a loss for the year
public companies and large proprietary companies
only companies listed on the stock exchange
questions.explanation: Public companies and large proprietary companies must generally prepare annual financial reports, have them audited and lodge them with ASIC, which gives investors and lenders reliable information. Sole traders and partnerships are not companies.

questions.stem: Under the Corporations Act 2001, the prohibition of insolvent trading means that a director must not:
options: allow the company to sell its assets to raise funds for working capital
allow the company to incur debts when it cannot pay its debts as they fall due
allow the company to borrow money from any bank without shareholders' approval
allow the company to pay a dividend in any year in which profit has fallen
questions.explanation: Directors have a duty to prevent the company incurring debts while insolvent, and can be personally liable if they breach it. This makes careful monitoring of liquidity and solvency a legal as well as a financial priority.

questions.stem: A company's directors see that it cannot pay its suppliers on time, but they keep ordering stock on credit, hoping trading will improve. What is the most significant risk?
options: the company's tax rate will rise to the full company rate
the directors may be personally liable for insolvent trading
the company will automatically become a sole trader
the company's suppliers must cancel all of its debts
questions.explanation: Incurring new debts when the company cannot pay its debts as they fall due may breach the insolvent trading prohibition, exposing directors personally. Limited liability protects shareholders, not directors who breach this duty.

questions.stem: Environmental, social and governance (ESG) reporting influences financial management mainly because:
options: it allows the business to avoid paying company tax on environmental projects
investors and lenders use it to judge risk before providing funds
it replaces the income statement and balance sheet for companies that publish it
it sets the price of the company's shares on the stock exchange each day
questions.explanation: Many investors and lenders consider environmental, social and governance performance when assessing long-term risk, so strong and honest ESG reporting can improve access to finance. It supplements, not replaces, financial statements.

questions.stem: A finance manager approves a large loan to buy new machinery, but the marketing team has not planned how to sell the extra output. Which problem does this show?
options: a breach of the prohibition of insolvent trading by the finance manager
a failure of investment appraisal caused by a rise in the exchange rate
a lack of alignment between finance decisions, other functions and strategy
a conflict between solvency and efficiency within the operations function
questions.explanation: Finance decisions should be aligned with the plans of marketing, operations and human resources, and with business strategy. Funding extra capacity that cannot be sold raises costs and debt without adding revenue.
